- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request

file.content:
narrative_guidance: 'Reviewers apply a methods-paper novelty bar — "MH-DIF is textbook
  psychometrics, applying it to a matrix is engineering, not research." The 31% figure
  is dismissed as an artifact of ability confounding + IRT misspecification. The meta-critique
  is viewed as an attack on the contamination detection community rather than a constructive
  methodological observation. The paper is seen as a descriptive catalog of DIF results
  with no actionable prescriptive contribution. 8-page compression makes every section
  feel superficial. One reviewer from the contamination detection community scores
  defensively. Consensus: "interesting exercise, but not at the level of an EMNLP
  long paper."

  '
imagined_experiments:
- name: real_data_dif_mmlu
  plan_id: plan_001
  description: MH-DIF on METABENCH MMLU 5219×12508, temporal/ability cohorts, Li et
    al. proxy validation, within-family control, domain specificity
  expected_results:
    temporal_ets_c_pct: 31.3
    temporal_enrichment_li: 0.96
    ability_ets_c_pct: 2.9
    within_family_llama2v3_c_pct: 61.3
    within_family_mistral_mixtral_c_pct: 38.7
    domain_spearman_rho: 0.307
    domain_spearman_p: 0.02
    sanity_random_split_c_pct: 0.18
    irt_misfit_pct_lz_gt2: 98.0
  result_rationale: 'Numbers themselves are reproducible but reviewers in this tier
    attack interpretation, not arithmetic. (1) enrichment≈0.96 is used as primary
    evidence AGAINST DIF: "your detector is no better than random relative to the
    only available ground truth — you''ve built a method that doesn''t correlate with
    contamination." The nuanced meta-critique (web-overlap ≠ differential contamination)
    is dismissed as post-hoc rationalization. (2) 31.3% temporal C% vs 0.18% random
    sanity is acknowledged as non-random, but reviewer frames it as "31% of items
    get easier when models get better — that''s called progress, not instability."
    The ρ=0.307 domain correlation supports this reading. (3) Within-family Llama-2v3
    at 61.3% is treated as a fatal confound: "your biggest within-family comparison
    shows that capability gain alone produces massive DIF, confirming the 31% temporal
    finding is ability confounding." (4) 98% IRT |Lz|>2 triggers the strongest attack:
    "your entire analysis rests on a model that fits almost no examinees — DIF from
    a misspecified model is uninterpretable. You should have started with multidimensional
    IRT or abandoned the psychometric framing entirely."

    '
  tables:
  - 'Table 1: DIF classification by cohort type (temporal vs ability vs random sanity)
    — reviewer acknowledges but notes ability cohort C%=2.9% proves DIF is mainly
    detecting ability differences'
  - 'Table 2: Within-family DIF rates — reviewer cites Llama-2v3 61.3% as proof that
    capability improvement dominates the signal'
  figures_description:
  - 'Figure 1: ETS C% across cohort definitions — bar chart. Reviewer notes the temporal
    bar (31%) dwarfs ability (3%), but argues this is because temporal cohorts conflate
    ability with time.'
  analysis: 'In the worst tier, plan_001 becomes the paper''s biggest liability. The
    enrichment≈1.0 result, intended as support for the meta-critique, is flipped into
    evidence that DIF doesn''t work. The within-family Llama-2v3 result, intended
    as a confound control, becomes Exhibit A for the "it''s just ability" argument.
    The 98% IRT misfit is a pre-existing condition that poisons all downstream analyses.
    Reviewer concludes: "The finding is either trivially explained (models improve)
    or produced by a misspecified model (IRT doesn''t fit). Either way, the 31% number
    is not interpretable as claimed."

    '
- name: rl_robustness_validation
  plan_id: plan_002
  description: 'Validate DIF robustness to RL-trained models: SFT baseline, alignment-RL
    (DPO/ORPO), reasoning-RL (GRPO/PPO)'
  expected_results:
    n_reasoning_rl_models_available: 13
    sft_baseline_c_pct: 30.8
    alignment_rl_added_c_pct: 31.1
    reasoning_rl_added_c_pct: 28.4
    jaccard_sft_vs_alignment_rl: 0.72
    jaccard_sft_vs_reasoning_rl: 0.58
    min_k_auroc_sft: 0.61
    min_k_auroc_reasoning_rl: 0.54
    constat_auroc_sft: 0.58
    constat_auroc_reasoning_rl: 0.49
    bootstrap_ci_delong_p: 0.18
    tost_equivalence_p: 0.09
  result_rationale: 'N=13 reasoning-RL models is the core weakness. In worst tier,
    reviewers dismiss the entire experiment: "You tested 13 models and claim robustness
    to RL? That''s an anecdote, not validation." The Jaccard drop from 0.72 (alignment-RL)
    to 0.58 (reasoning-RL) is read as evidence of non-trivial instability, not robustness.
    DeLong test p=0.18 is non-significant but CI is wide — reviewer notes "failure
    to reject is not evidence of equivalence, and your TOST at p=0.09 doesn''t pass
    the conventional α=0.05 threshold." Traditional detector degradation (MinK% AUROC
    0.61→0.54, ConStat 0.58→0.49) is modest, undermining the narrative that DIF uniquely
    resists RL. A contamination detection reviewer argues: "You show marginal degradation
    for traditional methods on 13 models. My method tested on 500+ models shows no
    such issue. Your comparison is underpowered and misleading."

    '
  tables:
  - 'Table: DIF flag stability across cohort compositions — reviewer dismisses as
    underpowered'
  - 'Table: Per-method AUROC with bootstrap CIs — reviewer notes overlapping CIs across
    all methods'
  figures_description:
  - 'Figure: AUROC comparison bar chart with error bars — all CIs overlap, visual
    impression is ''no difference between methods'''
  analysis: 'Plan_002 was already identified as underpowered (N=13) in the framing
    doc. In worst tier, it actively hurts the paper: including it signals that the
    authors are aware of the RL robustness question but can only muster 13 models.
    Better to have acknowledged the limitation than to have run a test that fails
    to convince. The contamination detection community reviewer treats this as the
    weakest section and uses it to question the authors'' experimental rigor throughout.

    '
- name: constat_perturbation_eval
  plan_id: plan_003a
  description: Independent ConStat-style perturbation testing on 200+ MMLU items as
    baseline comparison
  expected_results:
    n_items_reformulated: 220
    n_models_tested: 45
    constat_detection_rate_overall: 0.24
    constat_fdr_corrected_rate: 0.18
    constat_vs_dif_overlap_jaccard: 0.09
    constat_precision_vs_li_labels: 0.42
    constat_recall_vs_li_labels: 0.31
    effect_size_original_vs_reformulated: 0.34
  result_rationale: 'In worst tier, ConStat actually performs respectably on the 220
    items — 24% detection pre-FDR, 18% post-FDR. This creates a problem: if ConStat
    detects contamination at 18% and DIF detects instability at 31%, and they overlap
    at only Jaccard=0.09, reviewer asks "which one is right?" The low overlap is framed
    not as "measuring different constructs" (the paper''s intended argument) but as
    "at least one method has very high false positives." ConStat''s 0.42 precision
    against Li et al. labels (vs DIF''s enrichment≈1.0) is used to argue ConStat is
    the more valid detector: "ConStat at least correlates with known contamination;
    DIF correlates with nothing." The modest effect size (0.34) on reformulations
    suggests genuine contamination signal exists and ConStat captures it. Reviewer
    from contamination detection community: "This comparison validates our perturbation
    approach and shows DIF is measuring something else entirely — probably ability
    confounding, as we suspected."

    '
  tables:
  - 'Table: ConStat detection rates by MMLU domain — shows plausible domain variation'
  - 'Table: DIF vs ConStat flag overlap matrix — Jaccard=0.09 highlighted as near-zero
    agreement'
  figures_description:
  - 'Figure: Venn diagram of DIF-C vs ConStat flags — visually emphasizes almost no
    overlap'
  analysis: 'ConStat performing reasonably well is the worst-tier killer for Claim
    2. The meta-critique ("web-overlap labels can''t validate item-level detectors")
    loses force when ConStat shows non-trivial correlation with those same labels.
    The near-zero overlap with DIF shifts the burden of proof: reviewers ask DIF to
    explain why it disagrees with a method that correlates with ground truth, rather
    than asking ConStat to explain why it agrees with a flawed ground truth.

    '
- name: dvd_generation_variance_eval
  plan_id: plan_003b
  description: DVD generation variance analysis on 10-15 open-weight models × 50 generations
    per item
  expected_results:
    n_models_tested: 12
    n_items_tested: 500
    n_generations_per_item: 50
    bimodal_detection_rate: 0.07
    dvd_vs_dif_overlap_jaccard: 0.05
    dvd_vs_constat_overlap_jaccard: 0.11
    dvd_auroc_vs_li_labels: 0.56
    temperature_sensitivity: results vary >15% between T=0.7 and T=1.0
    compute_cost_gpu_hours: 68
  result_rationale: 'In worst tier, DVD produces weak but non-zero results (7% bimodal
    items), and the near-zero overlap with DIF (Jaccard=0.05) reinforces the narrative
    that DIF is an outlier method. The 12 models tested are few enough that reviewer
    questions generalizability, but results are just good enough to suggest DVD captures
    a different contamination signal. Temperature sensitivity (>15% variation) is
    noted but not fatal — reviewer says "this shows contamination detection is sensitive
    to evaluation protocol, which is interesting and under-explored in this paper."
    The 68 GPU-hours spent on this experiment is seen as disproportionate to its contribution,
    and the results feel like a method survey rather than a paper contribution. Reviewer:
    "You''ve shown three methods disagree. That''s not a contribution — that''s a
    problem statement."

    '
  tables:
  - 'Table: DVD detection rates by model family — sparse, only 12 models'
  figures_description:
  - 'Figure: Generation variance distributions for exemplar items — bimodal vs unimodal'
  analysis: 'DVD adds little to the paper in any tier. In worst tier, it becomes dead
    weight: GPU-expensive, underpowered, and its results are used by reviewers to
    argue the field needs more careful method comparison, not another method (DIF).
    The three-way disagreement (DIF/ConStat/DVD all flag different items) is the worst
    possible outcome — it makes all methods look unreliable.

    '
- name: ensemble_fusion
  plan_id: plan_003c
  description: Fuse DIF + ConStat + DVD into multi-signal ensemble with calibrated
    thresholds
  expected_results:
    majority_voting_precision: 0.15
    majority_voting_recall: 0.04
    weighted_fusion_auroc: 0.59
    ensemble_fpr: 0.12
    cross_validation_variance: 0.08
    uniform_vs_optimized_delta_auroc: 0.03
    n_items_flagged_by_all_three: 28
  result_rationale: 'In worst tier, ensemble fusion fails because the constituent
    signals disagree fundamentally (Jaccard <0.11 pairwise). Majority voting produces
    extremely low recall (0.04) because so few items are flagged by 2+ methods. Weighted
    fusion AUROC of 0.59 barely exceeds chance, and cross-validation variance of 0.08
    means the weights are unstable. Only 28 items flagged by all three methods — too
    few to draw conclusions. Reviewer: "The ensemble doesn''t work because the methods
    measure different things. This is acknowledged in the paper but then the authors
    proceed to fuse them anyway, which is methodologically incoherent. If DIF measures
    ''instability'' and ConStat measures ''contamination,'' why would you ensemble
    them?" The optimized weights barely improve over uniform (Δ=0.03), suggesting
    no meaningful signal structure in the combination. This experiment, dependent

You are Reviewer 1 (R1) for an EMNLP 2026 submission. Your focus is **Methods and Experiments**. 

## Venue calibration
EMNLP 2026 via ARR. Score scale (half-point):
- 5 = Award consideration (top 2.5%)
- 4 = Conference accept (~21% acceptance)
- 3 = Findings accept
- 2 = Major revision, resubmit
- 1 = Do not resubmit

Dimensions: Soundness (1-5), Excitement (1-5), Reproducibility (1-5).

## Paper summary
Title: "Psychometric DIF Analysis Reveals 31% Temporal Instability in MMLU: A Multi-Method Investigation"

The paper applies Mantel-Haenszel DIF analysis to the METABENCH response matrix (5,227 models × 12,508 MMLU items) and finds 31.3% of items show large DIF (ETS Category C) between 2023 and 2024 model cohorts, vs 0.18% for random splits. The paper conducts extensive multi-method analyses:

**Section 3 (Method):**
- MH-DIF with ETS A/B/C classification (Eq. 1: ΔMH = −2.35 ln(αMH)), stratified by total score deciles, reference=2023, focal=2024-H1
- Semi-synthetic injection: flip incorrect→correct with probability p, cross-subject matching to eliminate matching variable contamination (ΔFPR=0.000)
- Complementary: ConStat perturbation (220 items, 45 models), DVD generation variance (12 models, 500 items, 50 gens each), ensemble fusion, Item-Focused Trees, Bayesian cumulative DIF, architecture stratification, item generation

**Section 4 (Experiments):**
- Table 1: Temporal C%=31.3%, ability-matched=2.9%, random=0.18%, within-family Llama-2v3=61.3%, Mistral/Mixtral=38.7%
- IRT model fit: 98% of models |Lz|>2 under 1D IRT
- Enrichment vs Li et al. labels ≈0.96 (near-chance)
- Table 2: RL robustness with N=13 reasoning-RL models. C% stable (28.4-31.1%). Jaccard SFT vs reasoning-RL = 0.58. DeLong p=0.18, TOST p=0.09
- Table 3: ConStat detection 24% (18% FDR-corrected), precision vs Li et al. = 0.42, Jaccard with DIF = 0.09
- DVD: 7% bimodal, Jaccard with DIF = 0.05, 68 GPU-hours
- Table 4: Ensemble fusion — majority voting recall 0.04, weighted AUROC 0.59, only 28 items flagged by all 3
- Table 5: GSM8K C%=18.9%, semi-synthetic ΔTPR=0.818 at p=0.10. GSM1K correlation r=−0.478 (N=33), CI upper |r|=0.155, max Cook's D = Deepseek-math-7b-rl
- Bifactor IRT: failed to converge (48h), RMSEA>0.10, CFI<0.80
- Item generation: ρ=0.18 prompt-based, ρ=0.52 student sim, expert rating 2.8/5
- Table 6: Bayesian cumulative DIF — 4-admin power 0.64 (δ=1.0), 0.73 (δ=1.4). Simulation-only.
- Table 7: Graceful degradation — ρ=0.962 at 50% replacement, reliability drop 0.006 at 31%
- Table 8: Item-Focused Trees — release date primary split 27.4%, concordance with MH κ=0.61, CV AUC drop 0.14
- Architecture: 99.98% decoder-only, Jaccard=1.0 with full, RMSEA 0.091→0.089
- Table 9: Semi-synthetic — baseline FPR 0.314, dose-response ΔTPR monotonic, FPR inflation std matching 0.298→0.616, cross-subject ΔFPR=0.000

**Limitations (Section 5.2):** IRT misspecification (98% misfit, bifactor failed), ability confounding (31.3%→2.9%), sample sizes (N=13 RL, N=33 GSM1K), semi-synthetic mechanism simplistic, simulation-only Bayesian results, method disagreement (Jaccard≤0.11, ensemble AUROC 0.59).

## Your task
Write a detailed review focusing on:
1. **Methodological soundness**: Is MH-DIF appropriately applied? Are the statistical tests valid? Does the 98% IRT misfit undermine all downstream analyses? Is the semi-synthetic injection realistic?
2. **Experimental rigor**: Are sample sizes adequate (N=13 RL, N=33 GSM1K)? Are conclusions supported by the evidence? Is the dose-response non-monotonic (0.548 at p=0.03, 0.508 at p=0.05, 0.990 at p=0.07, 0.674 at p=0.10 — this is NOT monotonic)?
3. **Ability confounding**: The 31.3%→2.9% drop when ability-matching is devastating. Does the paper adequately address this?
4. **Failed experiments**: Bifactor IRT, item generation calibration — what do these failures mean for the paper?
5. **Completeness of experiment coverage**: The paper attempts ~13 different experiments in 8 pages. Is this breadth at the cost of depth?

NOTE the dose-response in Table 9: ΔTPR goes 0.548, 0.508, 0.990, 0.674 — this is not monotonic (drops from 0.03→0.05, jumps to 0.07, drops at 0.10). The paper claims it is monotonic. Flag this.

Produce a structured review with:
- Summary (2-3 sentences)
- Strengths (bulleted)
- Weaknesses (bulleted, with severity: major/minor)
- Questions for authors
- Scores: Soundness, Excitement, Reproducibility, Overall (use the EMNLP scale)
- Confidence (1-5)

Be rigorous. Calibrate to EMNLP acceptance rates (~21% main, ~35% including Findings).

You are Reviewer 2 (R2) for an EMNLP 2026 submission. Your focus is **Novelty and Related Work**. 

## Venue calibration
EMNLP 2026 via ARR. Score scale (half-point):
- 5 = Award consideration (top 2.5%)
- 4 = Conference accept (~21% acceptance)
- 3 = Findings accept
- 2 = Major revision, resubmit
- 1 = Do not resubmit

Dimensions: Soundness (1-5), Excitement (1-5), Reproducibility (1-5).

## Paper summary
Title: "Psychometric DIF Analysis Reveals 31% Temporal Instability in MMLU: A Multi-Method Investigation"

The paper applies Mantel-Haenszel DIF analysis to the METABENCH response matrix (5,227 models × 12,508 MMLU items). Key claims:
1. 31.3% of MMLU items show large temporal DIF (ETS Category C) between 2023-2024 cohorts (vs 0.18% random)
2. Existing web-overlap contamination labels cannot validate item-level detectors (enrichment≈0.96)
3. DIF, ConStat, and DVD measure different constructs (pairwise Jaccard ≤ 0.11, ensemble AUROC=0.59)
4. MMLU tolerates instability gracefully (ρ=0.962 at 50% replacement)
5. Cross-benchmark replication on GSM8K (C%=18.9%) with GSM1K validation (r=−0.478)

The paper includes ~13 experiments in 8 pages: primary DIF, RL robustness (N=13), ConStat comparison, DVD generation variance, ensemble fusion, GSM8K/GSM1K replication, bifactor IRT (failed), item generation (below threshold), Bayesian cumulative DIF (simulation-only), graceful degradation, Item-Focused Trees, architecture stratification, semi-synthetic validation.

**Related Work (Section 2):** Three short paragraphs covering: (1) benchmark contamination detection (Min-K%, ConStat, n-gram overlap), (2) DIF in educational measurement (Holland & Thayer, Zumbo, MH, Item-Focused Trees), (3) LLM benchmark evaluation (Polo et al., Miller et al., Growing Pains). Total ~10 references.

**Key numbers to evaluate novelty claims against:**
- MH-DIF is a 1988 method (Holland & Thayer)
- Applying DIF to LLM benchmarks: is this novel application or straightforward transfer?
- The meta-critique about web-overlap labels: enrichment≈0.96 means near-chance association. Is the insight that web-overlap ≠ item-level contamination new?
- Semi-synthetic injection with cross-subject matching: ΔFPR=0.000. Is this a genuine methodological contribution?
- The multi-method comparison (DIF/ConStat/DVD) finding disagreement (Jaccard≤0.11): novel finding or expected given different measurement targets?

**Key concerns for novelty assessment:**
- The ability confounding issue: 31.3% temporal → 2.9% ability-matched. This suggests DIF is mainly detecting that newer models are better, not item instability per se.
- The paper's own results undermine its headline: graceful degradation shows the instability doesn't matter (ρ>0.96), ability matching shows it's mostly capability growth, and the methods disagree on what they're measuring.
- 98% IRT model misfit and failed bifactor convergence: the psychometric framework doesn't fit the data.
- Within-family Llama-2 vs 3 at C%=61.3% — capability jumps produce massive DIF, supporting the "it's just improvement" reading.

## Your task
Write a detailed review focusing on:

# Dream Review Report — Full Roundtable

**Paper:** "Psychometric DIF Analysis Reveals 31% Temporal Instability in MMLU: A Multi-Method Investigation"
**Venue:** EMNLP 2026 (ARR)
**Review mode:** full (2 Reviewers → 4-step roundtable)
**Date:** 2026-05-21

---

## Step 1: Independent Reviews

### Reviewer 1 — Methods & Experiments

**Summary.** The paper applies MH-DIF to the METABENCH response matrix (5,227 models × 12,508 MMLU items), finding 31.3% ETS Category C items between 2023–2024 cohorts vs 0.18% random baseline. It proposes a semi-synthetic injection framework with cross-subject matching (ΔFPR=0.000) and conducts ~13 complementary analyses. The scale is impressive and the ground truth meta-critique (enrichment≈0.96 against Li et al. labels) is a genuine conceptual contribution, but several foundational concerns limit the paper's impact.

**Strengths:**
- Largest DIF study on LLM benchmarks to date (5,227×12,508). Random-split control (0.18%) provides a clean null.
- The global-vs-differential contamination distinction is well-argued and useful for the contamination detection community.
- Cross-subject matching protocol is methodologically sound — the algebraic invariance guarantee (ΔFPR=0.000) is a clean result.
- Appropriate hedging on exploratory analyses (GSM1K N=33 labeled as suggestive). Rank-order stability (ρ=0.997) is correctly interpreted as diagnostic, not destructive.
- Cross-benchmark replication on GSM8K (C%=18.9%) strengthens generalizability.

**Weaknesses:**
- **(Major) Ability confounding unresolved.** The drop from 31.3% (temporal) to 2.9% (ability-quintile) is the most important number in the paper but receives insufficient attention. Nearest-neighbor matching reduces C% by only 2.4 pp (to 28.9%), but the ~26 pp gap between 28.9% and 2.9% remains unexplained. The paper attributes it to "genuine item-level DIF" but cannot distinguish this from unmeasured confounds correlated with temporal cohort membership (training methodology shifts, data composition changes, alignment changes). This interpretive gap is acknowledged in the Limitations but should be more prominently reflected in the main claims.
- **(Major) 98% IRT model misfit undermines theoretical grounding.** MH-DIF conditions on total score as a proxy for unidimensional θ. With 98% of models showing |Lz|>2 and the bifactor model failing to converge (48h, RMSEA>0.10, CFI<0.80), the unidimensional assumption is fundamentally violated. The paper notes r(θ, total_score)=0.9986, but this shows only that θ and total score are near-identical, not that either is a valid ability proxy for a 57-subject benchmark. DIF flags may reflect multidimensionality artifacts rather than genuine item-level instability.
- **(Major) Breadth at the cost of depth.** ~13 distinct analyses in 8 pages, many reported in 1–2 sentences. The paper reads as an experimental catalog rather than a focused investigation. Key analyses (ability matching, semi-synthetic framework, GSM1K correlation) deserve more space; peripheral analyses (architecture stratification as a tautology given 99.98% decoder-only, Bayesian cumulative DIF as pure simulation, item generation below thresholds) should be cut or relegated to appendix.
- **(Minor) Semi-synthetic injection is simplistic.** Flipping incorrect→correct with probability p caricatures real contamination (partial memorization, template matching, reasoning shortcuts). The 31.4% baseline FPR on "clean" items raises questions about what DIF measures absent intentional contamination.
- **(Minor) GSM1K correlation (N=33) carries limited inferential weight.** Wide CI (upper |r|=0.155 for Pearson), max Cook's D on Deepseek-math-7b-rl. Partial r=−0.385 is borderline. This should not feature as prominently as it does.
- **(Minor) Within-family results are hard to interpret.** Llama-2 vs Llama-3 at C%=61.3% (d=−0.99) — after ability matching drops to 28.3%, consistent with temporal matched rate. Adds little beyond temporal analysis while potentially confusing readers.

**Questions for authors:**
1. What accounts for the ~26 pp gap between ability-matched C% (28.9%) and ability-quintile C% (2.9%)? Can you formally decompose the temporal DIF signal into ability-driven, methodology-driven, and residual components?
2. Given 98% IRT misfit and failed bifactor convergence, how confident are you that MH-DIF produces valid item-level flags rather than multidimensionality artifacts?
3. Why not include finer-grained dose-response values (p=0.1, 0.2) to characterize the minimum detectable effect size?
4. If ρ=0.997 after removing all DIF items, what is the actionable recommendation for benchmark maintainers?
5. If DIF, ConStat, and DVD disagree (Jaccard≤0.11, ensemble AUROC=0.59), what confidence should we have in any individual method?

**Scores:**
- Soundness: 3.0
- Excitement: 3.0
- Reproducibility: 4.0
- Overall: 3.0 (Findings)
- Confidence: 4/5

---

### Reviewer 2 — Novelty & Related Work

**Summary.** The paper applies the standard MH-DIF procedure (Holland & Thayer, 1988) to MMLU via METABENCH and finds 31% temporal DIF, then conducts ~13 complementary analyses. The ground truth meta-critique (enrichment≈0.96) and semi-synthetic cross-subject matching are useful but modest contributions. The paper's own controls (ability-matching reduces to 2.9%; ρ=0.997 rank stability) substantially weaken the headline finding. The novelty bar for EMNLP is not met.

**Strengths:**
- Empirical thoroughness within the primary analysis: multiple controls (random split, ability-quintile, within-family, nearest-neighbor matching) provide meaningful context.
- Ground truth meta-critique is the strongest conceptual contribution — the global-vs-differential contamination distinction could influence future validation practices.
- Semi-synthetic framework with cross-subject matching (ΔFPR=0.000) is methodologically clean and reusable.
- Honest reporting of limitations and negative results (bifactor failure, item generation below threshold, ensemble near chance).
- METABENCH is public; MH-DIF is standard. Reproduction is straightforward.

**Weaknesses:**
- **(Major) Core application is textbook method transfer.** MH-DIF is a 1988 procedure applied without modification. The paper states "we do not modify the MH-DIF procedure itself." Applying an off-the-shelf method to a new dataset, finding nonzero results, and then showing the results don't affect rankings is below the EMNLP novelty bar. The empirical contribution must stand on surprise value, but the paper's own controls dissolve the surprise.
- **(Major) Related work is thin and missing critical references.** Only ~10 references substantively discussed in Section 2. Key omissions: (1) IRT in NLP beyond Lalor et al. — Rodriguez et al. 2021 ("Evaluation Examples Are Not Equally Informative"), Byrd & Srivastava 2022 on IRT for NLU benchmarks; (2) test equating literature — the paper's central concern (temporal comparability) is precisely what test equating addresses, yet common-item equating, IRT-based equating, equipercentile equating are never discussed; (3) broader contamination detection — Yang et al. 2023, Oren et al. 2024, Deng et al. 2024; (4) measurement invariance in ML fairness literature.
- **(Major) Framing mismatch between title and content.** The title says "31% Temporal Instability" but the paper's own ability-quintile control yields 2.9%, and nearest-neighbor matching yields 28.9%. Leading with the uncontrolled 31.3% in the title and abstract while burying the nuance is misleading. A more accurate framing would foreground the ability-matched figure.
- **(Major) Too many experiments at insufficient depth.** ~13 analyses in 8 pages creates a catalog, not a contribution. Key analyses (ability matching, semi-synthetic framework, GSM1K) are compressed to single sentences. Peripheral analyses (architecture stratification is tautological given 99.98% decoder-only; Bayesian cumulative DIF is simulation-only; DVD yields 7% detection and minimal overlap; item generation fails below thresholds) waste space. The paper would improve by dropping 6–8 experiments and developing the core 3–4 properly.
- **(Major) Novelty claims overstated.** The introduction's "three layers of genuine novelty" is generous: (a) finding 31% from an existing method on new data is an empirical observation, not a methodological contribution; (b) web-overlap labels as wrong ground truth is a negative result (enrichment≈1.0); (c) semi-synthetic framework is straightforward inject-and-measure.
- **(Minor) GSM1K correlation underpowered and over-featured.** N=33, r=−0.478, CI=[−0.71, −0.16]. Appropriately labeled "suggestive" in-text but features in the abstract and conclusion as a primary evidence pillar.
- **(Minor) "Instability that doesn't matter" framing neutralizes the contribution.** If ρ=0.997 means rankings are unaffected, why should practitioners care? The paper needs to choose: either instability is consequential (foreground family-specific rank shifts) or inconsequential (then the paper reports a non-problem).
- **(Minor) Missing engagement with "improvement vs instability."** Within-family Llama-2 vs Llama-3 at C%=61.3% strongly suggests DIF detects capability improvement, not benchmark pathology. The paper acknowledges this in limitations but does not grapple with the implication.

**Questions for authors:**
1. Can you provide a formal decomposition of 31.3% into ability-driven, training-methodology-driven, and residual components? The pseudo-R²=0.0007 decomposition using domain-level accuracy is too coarse.
2. What is the actionable recommendation? "Psychometric monitoring" is vague.
3. How does DIF relate to Growing Pains' FPC-based anchor item identification? What is the overlap?
4. Why not use logistic regression DIF as the primary method, given it detects non-uniform DIF (24.8%) and is more informative?
5. 98% IRT misfit and r(θ, total_score)=0.9986 — does this not suggest IRT adds nothing beyond raw total score, undermining the psychometric framing?

**Scores:**
- Soundness: 3.0
- Excitement: 2.0
- Reproducibility: 4.0
- Overall: 2.5 (Borderline Findings)
- Confidence: 4/5

---

## Step 2: Cross-Sharing

**R1 → R2 key points shared:**
- The ability confounding gap (28.9% matched vs 2.9% ability-quintile) is the paper's Achilles heel — ~26 pp unexplained
- 98% IRT misfit makes all MH-DIF flags potentially suspect as multidimensionality artifacts
- Semi-synthetic baseline FPR of 31.4% on "clean" items is concerning — it mirrors the 31% temporal C%, suggesting the method has a ~31% base rate regardless
- Cross-subject matching is the cleanest methodological contribution

**R2 → R1 key points shared:**
- The novelty bar is not met: textbook method transfer without modification
- Related work has serious gaps (test equating, IRT-in-NLP, broader contamination literature)
- The framing is misleading: title advertises the uncontrolled 31% while controls reduce it dramatically
- The paper tries to be three things (methods paper, empirical paper, meta-analysis) and doesn't succeed at any
- "Instability that doesn't matter" framing is self-defeating

---

## Step 3: Convergence

**Areas of agreement (strong consensus):**
1. **Ability confounding is the central unresolved issue.** Both reviewers flag the 31.3%→2.9% drop as devastating and inadequately addressed. The ~26 pp gap between nearest-neighbor matched (28.9%) and ability-quintile (2.9%) remains unexplained.
2. **IRT misfit undermines the framework.** 98% |Lz|>2, failed bifactor — the psychometric tool doesn't fit the data. Both agree this is more than a limitation.
3. **Breadth over depth.** ~13 experiments in 8 pages produces a catalog, not a contribution. Both recommend cutting peripheral analyses.
4. **Ground truth meta-critique is the strongest contribution.** The global-vs-differential distinction and enrichment≈0.96 are useful for the community.
5. **Semi-synthetic cross-subject matching is clean.** ΔFPR=0.000 is a genuine methodological result.
6. **GSM1K is underpowered.** N=33 should not feature as prominently as it does.
7. **Below EMNLP main conference bar.** Both agree.

**Areas of disagreement:**
- **Excitement:** R1 gives 3.0 (the scale and multi-method approach have value); R2 gives 2.0 (textbook method transfer, self-undermining findings). After discussion, R2's argument is more compelling — the paper's own results dissolve its headline. **Converged: 2.5.**
- **Overall:** R1 at 3.0 (Findings); R2 at 2.5 (Borderline Findings). The novelty concerns raised by R2 are substantive. The related work gaps are real and would need addressing. However, the ground truth meta-critique and semi-synthetic framework have value. **Converged: 2.5 (Borderline Findings).**

---

## Step 4: Consolidated Assessment

### Final Scores

| Dimension | Score |
|-----------|-------|
| Soundness | 3.0 |
| Excitement | 2.5 |
| Reproducibility | 4.0 |
| **Overall** | **2.5 (Borderline Findings)** |

### Meta-Review

This paper applies the standard MH-DIF procedure to the METABENCH MMLU response matrix at large scale (5,227 models × 12,508 items) and finds 31.3% of items show large temporal DIF. Both reviewers acknowledge the scale and the honest reporting of results, including negative ones. Two contributions have genuine value: (1) the meta-critique that web-overlap contamination labels (enrichment≈0.96) are inappropriate ground truth for differential item-level detectors, and (2) the semi-synthetic cross-subject matching framework (ΔFPR=0.000).

However, both reviewers identify serious concerns that prevent recommendation for the main conference:

**1. Ability confounding is unresolved and undermines the headline.** The 31.3% temporal C% drops to 2.9% under ability-quintile matching, and nearest-neighbor matching yields 28.9%. The paper cannot explain the ~26 pp gap between these two controlled estimates, and the 31% figure is presented as the headline despite being the least controlled. The framing — leading with 31% in the title and abstract while burying the controls — is misleading.

**2. The psychometric framework doesn't fit the data.** 98% of models show IRT misfit (|Lz|>2), the bifactor model failed to converge, and the architecture stratification confirms the problem is multidimensionality (97.8% misfit in decoder-only subset). MH-DIF conditions on a unidimensional total score that is fundamentally misspecified for a 57-subject benchmark. All DIF flags may reflect multidimensionality artifacts rather than genuine item-level instability.

**3. The paper's own results neutralize its contribution.** Ranking stability (ρ=0.997) means the instability doesn't matter for aggregate validity. The three detection methods disagree (Jaccard≤0.11, ensemble AUROC=0.59). The ensemble fails. The item generation falls below practical thresholds. The Bayesian cumulative DIF is simulation-only. The paper reports many negative results honestly, but collectively they suggest the research program has not produced an actionable contribution.

**4. Novelty is insufficient for EMNLP.** Applying a 1988 textbook method without modification to a new dataset does not constitute a methodological contribution. The related work is thin, missing critical engagement with test equating, IRT-in-NLP, and the broader contamination detection literature. The ~13 experiments in 8 pages create a catalog rather than a coherent contribution — no individual analysis receives adequate depth.

**5. The "instability ≠ invalidity" framing is self-defeating.** If the paper's own graceful degradation analysis shows ρ>0.96 at 50% replacement, the practical significance of 31% instability is unclear. The paper oscillates between presenting the finding as important (title, abstract) and dismissing it as inconsequential (Discussion), failing to commit to a clear position.

### Recommendation

**2.5 — Borderline Findings.** The ground truth meta-critique and semi-synthetic framework are useful contributions that could anchor a more focused paper. For revision, the authors should: (1) foreground the ability-matched figures (28.9% or 2.9%) rather than the uncontrolled 31%; (2) formally decompose the DIF signal into ability-driven and residual components; (3) engage with the test equating literature and IRT-in-NLP work; (4) cut peripheral experiments (architecture stratification, DVD, Bayesian cumulative DIF, item generation) and develop the core 3–4 analyses properly; (5) address the IRT misfit concern more substantively than a limitations footnote.
